title: Perioperative Monitoring
summary: Set up basic monitoring, spot monitoring errors and react to a change in the patient's blood pressure.
scenario: You are preparing the monitoring for a patient scheduled for general anesthesia. Choose and check the monitors, interpret what you see, and respond correctly when the vital signs change during surgery.
objectives: Name the basic monitoring standard for general anesthesia
React to a change in vital signs

patient.procedure: Elective laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy under general anesthesia

history: No chronic illness, no regular medication
General anesthesia with a muscle relaxant is planned

steps.title: Basic standard
steps.prompt: Which set represents the basic monitoring standard for a general anesthetic?

options.text: Pulse oximetry, ECG, non-invasive blood pressure and capnography, with temperature monitored when significant changes are anticipated
Invasive arterial and central venous pressure for every patient
Pulse oximetry only, because it shows both oxygenation and ventilation

steps.explanation: Basic standards cover oxygenation (pulse oximetry), ventilation (capnography), circulation (ECG and blood pressure) and temperature when clinically relevant. Pulse oximetry alone shows oxygenation, not ventilation.
steps.takeaway: Oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, temperature. One monitor cannot cover all four.

steps.title: Prepare the monitors
steps.instruction: Select the monitoring equipment to prepare for this patient.

items.label: ECG electrodes and leads
items.why: Continuous ECG is a basic standard.

items.label: Blood pressure cuff of the correct size
items.why: A wrongly sized cuff gives wrong readings.

items.label: Temperature probe
items.why: Temperature changes are expected during anesthesia.

items.label: Peripheral nerve stimulator
items.why: A muscle relaxant is planned, so neuromuscular function should be monitored.

items.label: Pulmonary artery catheter
items.why: Not indicated for this healthy patient.

items.label: Invasive arterial line kit
items.why: Not routinely indicated for an ASA I patient and this procedure.

steps.explanation: Prepare the basic monitors plus a nerve stimulator because a muscle relaxant is planned. Invasive monitoring is reserved for patients or procedures that need it.
steps.takeaway: Match the monitors to the patient and the plan.

steps.title: Confirming ventilation
steps.situation: The patient has been intubated. Monitor: SpO₂ 99%, HR 72, BP 112/68, EtCO₂ 37 mmHg with a regular capnogram.
steps.prompt: Which finding BEST confirms that the patient is being ventilated effectively?

options.text: A regular capnogram waveform with a normal end-tidal CO₂ value

steps.explanation: Capnography directly shows exhaled CO₂ and therefore ventilation. SpO₂ can stay high for a while even when ventilation stops, especially after pre-oxygenation.
steps.takeaway: Capnography shows ventilation. SpO₂ lags behind.

steps.title: Monitoring set-up
steps.instruction: Select every entry that shows a monitoring problem.
steps.prompt: Review the current monitoring set-up. Which entries are problems?

items.label: Blood pressure cuff size appropriate for arm
Alarms muted to avoid disturbing the surgeon
items.why: Alarms are a safety net. They must stay audible with appropriate limits.

items.label: SpO₂ probe on the same arm as the blood pressure cuff (signal drops at every inflation)
items.why: Cuff inflation interrupts the pulse oximeter signal. Use the other arm or another site.

steps.explanation: Muted alarms remove an important safety net, and placing the SpO₂ probe on the cuff arm causes repeated signal loss.
steps.takeaway: Alarms on, probe and cuff on different limbs.

steps.title: How often?
steps.prompt: At minimum, how often should blood pressure and heart rate be evaluated during general anesthesia according to the ASA basic monitoring standard?

options.text: Once at induction and once at emergence

steps.explanation: The ASA standard says arterial blood pressure and heart rate should be evaluated at least every five minutes during anesthesia. Institutional protocols may require more frequent checks.
steps.takeaway: Blood pressure and heart rate at least every 5 minutes.

steps.title: Falling blood pressure
steps.situation: 45 minutes into surgery. The monitor now shows BP 82/48 and HR 112. The reading 5 minutes ago was 110/66.

options.text: Inform the anesthesiologist immediately and help verify the reading (cuff, trace) while looking for causes such as bleeding or a change in position
options.consequence: The anesthesiologist is informed early and the reading is checked at the same time.

options.text: Recycle the cuff and wait for the next reading before telling anyone
options.consequence: Verifying is reasonable, but waiting to inform the anesthesiologist delays the response to a real trend.

options.text: Assume it is an artifact and ignore it
options.consequence: A clear change in trend, together with a rising heart rate, must not be ignored.

options.text: Give a medication to raise the pressure without instruction
options.consequence: Medication decisions belong to the anesthesiologist. Acting alone is unsafe.

steps.explanation: A sharp fall in blood pressure with a rising heart rate is a significant change. Tell the anesthesiologist immediately while you verify the reading and look at possible causes.
steps.takeaway: Report significant changes early. Treatment decisions belong to the anesthesiologist.
